## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.59929.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.59929.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

Individuals show heritable variation in gene expression, which is associated with disease susceptibility. In contrast to many other studies that have focused on mapping associations between genetic and gene regulatory variation, the current work addresses group dispersion/variance of gene expression among samples as well as the evolutionary processes that shape differences in gene expression between individuals, in both humans and chimpanzees. Using computational deconvolution, the authors demonstrate that cell-type heterogeneity is an important component of expression variability, with significant overlap of orthologous genes associated with eQTLs in both species. The conclusion is that gene expression variability in humans and chimpanzees often evolves under similar evolutionary pressures.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Gene expression variability in human and chimpanzee populations share common determinants" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Detlef Weigel as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Charles G Danko (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to either limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary:

This is a solid study, with a large sample size, identifying quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) in humans and chimpanzees, using gene expression data from primary heart samples. The authors complemented the analysis of gene expression with a comparative eQTL mapping, as opposed to relying on mean expression levels, as most comparative studies like this one do. Also unlike many studies focused on mapping associations between genetic and gene regulatory variation, the authors paid attention to the group dispersion/variance of gene expression among samples as well as the evolutionary processes that shape the differences in gene regulation between individuals. The calculation of power for discovering differentially expressed genes as a function of sample size at the beginning of the paper is a thoughtful analysis that is useful to many in the community. All of the analyses are extremely thorough and well-executed. The statistical tests are appropriate and rigorous. Results are interpreted in a conservative fashion.

The main limitation is that the authors are not able to conclusively disambiguate between different causes of dispersion. Genetics, cell type, and technical variation may all contribute to dispersion. The authors state this very clearly throughout the manuscript. In part, this may reflect the authors' underselling their results somewhat. But in part, this really does reflect reality: Cell type is a major confounder that may provide false signals in other analyses.

Revisions for this paper:

The reviewers suggested a number of potential additions to clarify current results or build upon them. I will leave it up to the authors to decide which are worth including in their revision.

1) The first test authors conducted is to identify differentially variable (DV) genes. A total of 2658 DV genes were identified. The problem of the result is that almost equal number of up- and down-regulated DV genes symmetrically distributed around DV=0. Often, this is an indication of a lack of biological signals in data analysis. This might be due to the pooling of gene groups with diverse functionality together. Therefore, this reviewer suggests that authors should break down genes into subgroups to detail the up and down-regulatory patterns with the hope that some of the gene groups give interpretable results

2) The second test is to correlate the higher coding sequence conservation with lower dispersion. Again, the positive result is not unexpected. There are many indirect and/or confounding factors that may explain the effect. This reviewer, however, understands it is impossible to control them all (also authors have attempted to address some of them in the next few tests). However, here it is better to add exploratory analyses for genes in different functional groups and also give examples of outlier genes that do not follow the rule.

3) The third test is to examine the correlation between gene expression variability with single-cell type heterogeneity of samples. Authors first used Tabula Muris dataset to show dispersion is strongly correlated with cell-type specificity/diversity. If this is true, then the point that authors really wanted to demonstrate is, in fact, hampered. Authors might really want to show the "true" single-cell variability (see, for example, PMID: 31861624) is correlated with the level of group variance of gene expression.

4) The fourth test authors conducted is to show that dN/dS and Pn/Ps ratios of genes are correlated with gene expression variability (variance). However, because of the existence of heterogeneity of cell-type composition in samples, any correlation observed may be utterly biased by this single uncontrollable confounding factor. Furthermore, heart tissues contain an over-abundant expression of genes encoded in the mitochondrial genome. The expression level of these mt-genes may vary substantially between samples and reflect the health status of primary sample donors. PEER normalization may have to take this into account as a covariant.

5) Several other tests authors performed are around eQTLs (eGene overlap and eSNP overlap) between the two species. These are typical tests evolutionary biologists usually try to do whenever data are available. However, the issues with these types of tests are the low power in general. More importantly, in order to be consistent with previous tests which are all around the explanation of gene expression variance, this part should address the overlap between expression vQTLs in humans and chimps.

6) I would like to see more discussion about the inter-relatedness of the chimpanzees in the analysis of gene expression. Is that contributing to the power of the DE analysis, which has really high numbers of DE genes. That may certainly be due to the large samples size, but should be addressed. Related to that, the support that the gene-wise dispersion estimates are well correlated in humans and chimpanzees overall (Figure 1C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) seems qualitative. It looks like the chimpanzees might have less dispersion overall?

7) What do the authors think these findings mean for study systems outside of humans and captive chimpanzees? Both on the technical level (e.g. sample size), and for how their approach could be helpful outside of these species. Generalizing this approach would broaden the impact and audience of the paper.

8) Did the authors test directly whether eQTLs were enriched in genes with a high dispersion? I could not find this going back through the paper. This seems almost trivially likely to be true. I may have missed this result? Or did the authors worry this is too likely to be confounded with cell type? Either way, this seems like a result that may be useful to show even if the authors did acknowledge that it was likely to be confounded.

9) Did the authors consider looking for cell-type QTLs? They state several times in the paper the possibility that genetic factors may influence cell types. They have enough data – at least in human – to obtain QTLs for specific cell types, as others have done (Marderstein et al., 2020; Donovan et al., 2020). If these cell type QTLs were enriched near genes with a high dispersion, this may bolster the author's argument that genetic factors underlie dispersion by affecting cell type composition.

10) The scRNA-seq reference used for estimating cell types in heart tissue was derived from mice. Could this lead the authors to underestimate the degree to which cell types drive dispersion in genes that are variable between human and chimp? Genes that are variable between human/ chimp may also be more likely to be variable between either species and mouse, and perhaps this variability has led to them becoming more/ less of a marker of a specific cell population (and hence their dispersion in primates does not correlate with cell type specificity in mouse).

11) Have the authors tried estimating dispersion on top of what is expected based on differences in cell type? There are several strategies that might work for this: There are new strategies for estimating a posterior of cell type specific expression from a bulk sample, conditional on scRNA-seq data as prior information (Chu and Danko, 2020). These cell type specific expression estimates could then be analyzed for dispersion. Alternatively, it may also work to regress the estimated proportion of each cell type out of the dispersion estimates. While there are certainly a lot of pitfalls with using these strategies, especially in the setting shown here (all of this would work better if there were species matched reference data), they might provide an avenue for depleting the contribution of cell type differences from dispersion estimates.

12) Can the authors add a dotted line to show the shape of the distribution for genes with low dispersion, or where dispersion is shared in both human and chimpanzee, in Figure 4B? Is this different from genes that are dispersed in either chimp or human?

claims.claim: 8,880 differentially expressed genes were identified between species at FDR < 0.05.
claims.source: Using a linear model framework (see Materials and methods), we identified 8880 differentially expressed (DE) genes between species (FDR < 0.05), including 6,409 DE genes with effect sizes smaller than a twofold change (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the number of DE genes identified using statistical analysis.

claims.claim: 6,409 differentially expressed genes have effect sizes smaller than a twofold change.
claims.source: Using a linear model framework (see Materials and methods), we identified 8880 differentially expressed (DE) genes between species (FDR < 0.05), including 6,409 DE genes with effect sizes smaller than a twofold change (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of DE genes with small effect sizes.

claims.claim: The number of individuals, not sequencing depth, is the primary driver of power to detect inter-species differences in gene expression.
claims.source: As expected, we found that the number of individuals, not sequencing depth (within the range of 10M to >25M reads per sample), is the primary driver of power to detect inter-species differences in gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–O).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports findings from subsampling analyses comparing sample size and sequencing depth effects.

claims.claim: Comparative studies with small sample sizes are underpowered but their reports of differentially expressed genes are generally robust.
claims.source: Our results indicate that while comparative studies with small sample sizes are underpowered, their reports of differentially expressed genes are generally robust.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the subsampling analysis about the robustness of small sample studies.

claims.claim: A study with only four individuals from each species identified a median of 1,373 DE genes at FDR < 0.05.
claims.source: For example, when we used a sample size of only four chimpanzee individuals and four human individuals, we identified a median of 1,373 (869–2131 interquartile range across 100 resamples) DE genes (FDR < 0.05), or just 15% (10–24% IQR) of the genes identified as DE in the analysis of the full set of samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports specific results from subsampling analysis with n=4 per species.

claims.claim: Studies with four individuals per species capture only a median of 5% of DE genes with effect sizes smaller than a twofold change.
claims.source: Furthermore, a study with only four individuals from each species is particularly underpowered to identify subtle inter-species differences (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), only capturing a median of 5% (2–12% IQR) of the DE genes with effect sizes smaller than a twofold change.
claims.evidence: The manuscript quantifies the power to detect small effect size DE genes in small sample studies.

claims.claim: Estimated effect sizes in small sample studies are typically upwardly biased due to winner's curse effects.
claims.source: In addition, of the DE genes identified at this sample size, the estimated magnitude effect sizes are typically upwardly biased (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E) due to the winner's curse effects (Göring et al., 2001; Ioannidis, 2008), which particularly affect under-powered study designs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites literature on winner's curse and shows empirical evidence of this bias.

claims.claim: At small sample sizes with FDR of 5%, the empirically estimated false discovery rate is a median of 2%.
claims.source: However, even at this small sample size, the false positive rate associated with the classification of DE genes is well calibrated; when we used an FDR of 5% to classify genes as DE between the species, we empirically estimated a median of 2% (1–5% IQR) false discoveries based on the gold standard reference.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports empirical FDR estimates from subsampling analysis.

claims.claim: Some of the chimpanzees collected are first-degree relatives.
claims.source: Considering that some of the chimpanzees we collected data from are first-degree relatives, we wondered if the presence of highly related chimpanzee samples plays a meaningful role in the interspecies DE comparisons.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states that relatedness exists among chimpanzee samples.

claims.claim: Technical factors such as RNA extraction batch play a larger role in explaining gene expression variance than inter-relatedness.
claims.source: We found that technical factors, such as RNA extraction batch, play a larger role in explaining gene expression variance (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D) than the inter-relatedness.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from variance partitioning analysis.

claims.claim: The presence of inter-related samples plays a minimal role in altering interspecies DE analyses.
claims.source: Furthermore, we repeated the DE analysis procedures with subsamples of only the inter-related chimpanzee individuals, and did not find any meaningful difference in number of DE genes or estimated false discovery rate compared to subsamples of less related individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–F). We conclude that the presence of inter-related samples plays a minimal role in altering interspecies DE analyses.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from DE analysis with different levels of relatedness and draws a conclusion.

claims.claim: Overdispersion was estimated for each gene in chimpanzees and humans separately using a negative binomial regression model.
claims.source: To do so, we estimated overdispersion for each gene in chimpanzees and humans separately (see Materials and methods). Briefly, we assumed that the measurement process is captured by Poisson sampling, and that true gene expression follows a Gamma distribution. These assumptions are supported by theory (Pachter, 2011) and empirical data (Marioni et al., 2008). Accordingly, we used a negative binomial regression model to fit the RNA-seq data (22,23).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical model used for variability estimation with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Overdispersion is strongly correlated with mean expression.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings (Ecker et al., 2017; Eling et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2010), we observed that overdispersion is strongly correlated with mean expression, due to reasons which may be technical or biological in nature.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an observation consistent with prior literature.

claims.claim: Mean expression was regressed out from overdispersion estimates to obtain a mean-corrected summary of variability called 'dispersion'.
claims.source: To understand the properties of gene expression variability that are independent of mean gene expression level, we regressed out the mean from the overdispersion estimates, to obtain a gene-wise mean-corrected summary of variability, hereafter referred to as 'dispersion' (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the method for calculating dispersion.

claims.claim: 2,658 inter-species differentially dispersed genes were identified at FDR < 0.1.
claims.source: In total, we identified 2658 inter-species differentially dispersed genes (FDR < 0.1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the number of differentially dispersed genes identified.

claims.claim: Differentially dispersed genes are generally not differentially expressed.
claims.source: Inter-species differences in mean expression levels cannot explain this finding, as differentially dispersed genes are generally not differentially expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states that differential dispersion is independent of differential expression.

claims.claim: Gene-wise dispersion estimates are well correlated in humans and chimpanzees (R = 0.60).
claims.source: Despite the identification of thousands of differentially dispersed genes between the species, gene-wise dispersion estimates are well correlated in humans and chimpanzees overall (R = 0.60, Figure 2C), suggesting similar determinants of variability in the two species.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation coefficient and interprets its meaning.

claims.claim: Lower dispersion in expression levels is associated with higher protein coding conservation.
claims.source: Indeed, when we ranked and grouped genes by degree of protein coding conservation (assessed by percent amino acid identity between human and chimpanzee; Figure 3A), or by the ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous codon changes (dN/dS) across mammals (Figure 3B), we found that lower dispersion in expression levels is associated with higher protein coding conservation.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an association between dispersion and coding conservation metrics.

claims.claim: The trend of lower dispersion with higher conservation is most significant for genes in immune function categories.
claims.source: This trend is most significant for genes in functional categories (Gene Ontology; GO categories) related to immune function (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with immune-related genes being targets of rapid evolution by diversifying selection pressures, which may increase dispersion.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from GO category analysis and provides an interpretation.

claims.claim: Loss-of-function-intolerant genes have lower dispersion than loss-of-function-tolerant genes.
claims.source: To further establish the relationship between evolutionary coding conservation and dispersion, we utilized the prevalence of genetic diversity data from humans to categorize genes as loss-of-function-tolerant (ExAC pLI score <0.1) or loss-of-function-intolerant (ExAC pLI score >0.9) (Lek et al., 2016). We found that the expression of loss-of-function-intolerant genes is associated with lower dispersion (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an association between pLI scores and dispersion with citation to the data source.

claims.claim: TATA box genes are associated with higher dispersion.
claims.source: Finally, consistent with previous reports (de Jong et al., 2019; Hagai et al., 2018; Ravarani et al., 2016), we found that genes with TATA boxes are associated with higher dispersion (Figure 3D), potentially because TATA boxes are associated with higher transcriptional noise at the molecular level (Blake et al., 2006; Raser and O'Shea, 2004; Ravarani et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an observation consistent with prior literature and provides citations.

claims.claim: TATA box genes are enriched among cell-type-specific genes.
claims.source: However, a possible technical explanation for this observation is that TATA box genes are enriched among cell-type-specific genes (Schug et al., 2005) and cell-type heterogeneity between individuals or samples could contribute to the observed dispersion.
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites literature on TATA box gene properties and suggests an alternative explanation.

claims.claim: Genes with housekeeping functions are among the most enriched gene categories associated with low dispersion.
claims.source: We found that genes with housekeeping functions universal to all cell-types, such as genes related to transcription initiation and tRNA modification, are among the most enriched gene categories associated with low dispersion (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from gene set enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Genes with high dispersion are enriched for cardiovascular related functions.
claims.source: Conversely, genes with high dispersion are enriched for categories like fibrinolysis (the breakdown of blood clots), oxygen sensing, and other cardiovascular related functions (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from gene set enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: The most highly dispersed genes in bulk samples have more cell-type-specific expression in single-cell RNA-seq datasets.
claims.source: Qualitatively, we observed that the most highly dispersed genes in our bulk chimpanzee and human samples have more cell-type-specific expression among the nine heart cell types identified in Tabula Muris (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports observations from comparing bulk dispersion to single-cell data.

claims.claim: The lowest dispersed genes are more evenly expressed across cell types.
claims.source: Conversely, the lowest dispersed genes are more evenly expressed across cell types (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports observations from comparing bulk dispersion to single-cell data.

claims.claim: Dispersion is strongly correlated with cell-type-specificity (R = 0.32, p<2×10−16).
claims.source: More generally, when we summarized the level of cell-type-specific expression for each gene as a single summary statistic, τ (Kryuchkova-Mostacci and Robinson-Rechavi, 2016; Yanai et al., 2005), we found that dispersion is strongly correlated with cell-type-specificity (R = 0.32, p<2×10−16; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation with statistical significance and cites the method used.

claims.claim: The correlation between cell-type-specificity and dispersion may be downwardly biased due to using mouse heart data.
claims.source: Notably, the degree of cell-type-specificity is derived from data from mouse hearts, which may have diverged cell type expression profiles compared with primates. The correlation between cell-type-specificity and dispersion may therefore be downwardly biased as a result of error in estimating the true degree of cell-type-specificity of genes expressed primate hearts.
claims.evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a potential limitation in the analysis.

claims.claim: Cell type proportions between chimpanzee and human hearts are qualitatively similar.
claims.source: As expected, cell type proportions between chimpanzee and human hearts are qualitatively similar, although much inter-individual variation exists in both species for particular cell types, such as cardiac muscle cells and myofibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from cell type deconvolution analysis.

claims.claim: Deconvoluted expression profiles for different cell types cluster tightly by cell type rather than species.
claims.source: We found that the deconvoluted expression profiles for different cell types cluster tightly by cell type rather than species, as expected.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports clustering results from deconvoluted data.

claims.claim: Dispersion estimates from deconvoluted data cluster in a pattern more strongly influenced by species than by cell type.
claims.source: Interestingly, the dispersion estimates cluster in a complex pattern that is more strongly influenced by species. This is consistent with the idea that genetic variation, which nearly completely segregates by species, plays a meaningful role is explaining dispersion when cell composition variation is corrected for.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports clustering results and provides an interpretation.

claims.claim: Inter-individual dispersion in humans and chimpanzees is driven by genetic differences as well as cell type heterogeneity between samples.
claims.source: Put together, these analyses indicate that the levels of inter-individual dispersion we observed in humans and chimpanzees, and the high similarity in dispersion observed across species, are driven genetic differences as well as cell type heterogeneity between samples.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from multiple analyses.

claims.claim: The estimated fraction of cardiac muscle cells is highly correlated between atrial appendage and left ventricle samples from matched individuals.
claims.source: We found that the estimated fraction of cardiac muscle cells, the most common cell type in both tissue sections, is highly correlated between atrial appendage and left ventricle samples from matched individuals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from analyzing matched tissue samples.

claims.claim: Individual level factors generally explain more variance in cell type composition than tissue level factors.
claims.source: We used a linear mixed model (Hoffman and Schadt, 2016) to quantify the contribution of individual level versus tissue level factors to explain cell type composition estimates, and found that the individual level factor generally explains more variance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from variance partitioning analysis with citation to the method.

claims.claim: Sample-to-sample differences captured by dispersion estimates are driven largely by true differences between individuals rather than technical differences.
claims.source: We interpret this as strong evidence that the sample-to-sample differences captured by our dispersion estimates are driven largely by true differences between individuals, rather than random technical differences in sample acquisition and dissection.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the variance partitioning results.

claims.claim: The interspecies difference in dispersion is much less likely to be driven by cell type heterogeneity.
claims.source: Importantly, we find that the interspecies difference in dispersion is much less likely to be driven by cell type heterogeneity, although there is a relatively small but significant correlation with τ (R = 0.07, p=2.2×10−12; Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation and interprets its implications.

claims.claim: Genes more variable in human are enriched for mitotic regulators.
claims.source: We found that genes more variable in human are enriched for mitotic regulators (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from gene set enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: The enrichment for mitotic regulators may reflect the highly variable life histories in GTEx samples.
claims.source: Given evidence that ischemia may induce mitosis in adult mammalian cardiac cells (Kajstura et al., 1998; Kimura et al., 2017; Nakada et al., 2017), the enrichment for mitotic regulators may reflect the highly variable life histories in GTEx samples, a large fraction of which are sourced from organ donors with ischemic cardiovascular disease.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Genes related to immune function are more variable in chimpanzee.
claims.source: Conversely, we found that genes related to immune function are more variable in chimpanzee.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from gene set enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Genes with particularly low dispersion in human compared to chimpanzee display more constraint at the coding level in human than in chimpanzee.
claims.source: More specifically, we expect that genes with particularly low dispersion in human compared to chimpanzee will also display more constraint at the coding level in human than in chimpanzee.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states a hypothesis to be tested.

claims.claim: High-coverage whole genome sequencing was performed on 39 chimpanzee samples with >30X genome coverage obtained in all samples.
claims.source: We obtained human genotype data from the GTEx consortium, and chimpanzee data by performing high-coverage whole genome sequencing on the 39 chimpanzee samples used in this study (>30X genome coverage obtained in all samples, Supplementary file 2); these data represent roughly a 50% increase in the number of high-coverage Pan troglodytes genomes currently available (de Manuel et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of new genomic data with citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Nearly 2.9 million novel chimpanzee SNPs with MAF greater than 10% were identified.
claims.source: We used the sequencing data to identify nearly 2.9 million novel chimpanzee SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF) greater than 10%.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the number of SNPs identified from the sequencing data.

claims.claim: Loss-of-function tolerant genes have higher Pn/Ps than loss-of-function intolerant genes.
claims.source: As expected, we found that loss-of-function tolerant genes have higher Pn/Ps than loss-of-function intolerant genes (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an expected result from analyzing polymorphism data.

claims.claim: The inter-species ratio of Pn/Ps is positively correlated with the difference in gene expression dispersion between species.
claims.source: When we compared Pn/Ps between humans and chimpanzees, we found that the inter-species ratio of Pn/Ps is positively correlated with the difference in gene expression dispersion between species (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation between genetic and expression variability metrics.

claims.claim: Genes with higher dispersion in chimpanzees than in humans have a higher abundance of non-synonymous polymorphisms in chimpanzees compared to humans.
claims.source: That is, on average, genes with higher dispersion in chimpanzees than in humans have a higher abundance of non-synonymous polymorphisms (Pn/Ps) in chimpanzees compared to the orthologous genes in humans.
claims.evidence: The manuscript interprets the correlation between Pn/Ps ratio and dispersion difference.

claims.claim: Inter-species differences in selection pressures at polymorphic loci play a role in the observed inter-species differences in expression dispersion.
claims.source: This suggests that inter-species differences in selection pressures at polymorphic loci play a role in the observed inter-species differences in expression dispersion.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the Pn/Ps analysis.

claims.claim: 310 eGenes were identified in chimpanzee hearts at FDR < 0.1.
claims.source: Using this approach, we identified 310 eGenes in chimpanzee hearts (FDR < 0.1; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the number of eGenes identified in chimpanzees.

claims.claim: Chimpanzee eQTL SNPs are enriched near transcription start sites.
claims.source: Consistent with previous eQTL studies in primates (Jasinska et al., 2017; Pickrell et al., 2010; Tung et al., 2015; Veyrieras et al., 2008), we found that the chimpanzee eQTL SNPs are enriched near transcription start sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an observation consistent with prior literature.

claims.claim: There is no significant overlap of eGenes between humans and chimpanzees when considering one-to-one orthologs tested in both species using the full GTEx dataset.
claims.source: When considering only one-to-one orthologs tested for eGenes in both species, there is no significant overlap of eGenes in the two species (Odds Ratio = 1.03, p=0.46, hypergeometric test, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical test result for eGene overlap.

claims.claim: When using similar sample sizes, there is a greater overlap of eGenes between humans and chimpanzees than expected by chance.
claims.source: When we compared lists of eGenes identified in humans and chimpanzees using similar sample sizes, we found a greater overlap of eGenes in the two species than expected by chance (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from subsampling analysis to account for power differences.

claims.claim: Of the top 500 significant GTEx eGenes, 21 are also found to be eGenes in chimpanzee at FDR < 0.1, a significant enrichment.
claims.source: Specifically, of the top 500 significant GTEx eGenes (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 3C), 21 are also found to be eGenes in chimpanzee (FDR < 0.1), a significant enrichment (Odds Ratio = 2.05, p=0.003, hypergeometric test).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant overlap of eGenes.

claims.claim: Species-specific eGenes have higher species-specific dispersion.
claims.source: Importantly, we found that species-specific eGenes have higher species-specific dispersion (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an association between eGene classification and dispersion.

claims.claim: eGenes identified in chimpanzees but not humans have higher dispersion in chimpanzees and vice versa.
claims.source: That is, eGenes identified in chimpanzees but not humans have higher dispersion in chimpanzees and vice versa (p=3.7×10−11; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant association.

claims.claim: Within each species, eGenes tend to have higher dispersion than non-eGenes.
claims.source: Furthermore, within each species, eGenes tend to have higher dispersion than non-eGenes (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison of dispersion between eGenes and non-eGenes.

claims.claim: The observation that more eGenes are shared among humans and chimpanzees than expected by chance suggests that the regulation of these genes evolves under less evolutionary constraint.
claims.source: Furthermore, the observation that more eGenes are shared among humans and chimpanzees than expected by chance suggests that the regulation of these genes evolves under less evolutionary constraint.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the eGene overlap results.

claims.claim: eGenes have higher inter-species differences in expression levels than non-eGenes.
claims.source: We found that eGenes have higher inter-species differences in expression levels than non-eGenes (Figure 7A), and eGenes identified in both species have even larger differences in mean expression levels between species than eGenes identified only in chimpanzees or humans.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison of differential expression between eGene categories.

claims.claim: eGenes tend to have lower levels of coding conservation in both species.
claims.source: Furthermore, eGenes tend to have lower levels of coding conservation in both species, as measured by amino acid identity between human and chimpanzee (Figure 7B) or dN/dS across mammals (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports associations between eGene status and coding conservation metrics.

claims.claim: The 21 genes identified as shared eGenes are strongly enriched for immune response genes, including MHC genes.
claims.source: We found that these genes are strongly enriched for immune response genes, including major histocompatibility complex (MHC) genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: The enrichment of immune genes among shared eGenes is consistent with immune genes evolving under strong directional and balancing selection pressures across vertebrates.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with previous reports that immune genes evolve under strong directional and balancing selection pressures across vertebrates, in part to respond to ever-evolving pathogen challenges (Ejsmond and Radwan, 2015; Hagai et al., 2018; Lam et al., 2017; Shultz and Sackton, 2019).
claims.evidence: The manuscript interprets the enrichment result in the context of prior literature.

claims.claim: 148 chimpanzee-specific eGenes were identified and are significantly enriched for transcriptional regulation terms.
claims.source: We identified 148 chimpanzee-specific eGenes, which we found to be significantly enriched for transcriptional regulation terms (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports results from gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: A previous study identified 125 trans-species polymorphic haplotypes outside of the MHC region that are shared between chimpanzee and human.
claims.source: A previous study identified 125 trans-species polymorphic haplotypes outside of the MHC region that are shared between chimpanzee and human, all but two of which are in noncoding regions (Leffler et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that identified trans-species polymorphisms.

claims.claim: Genes nearest to trans-species SNPs have higher median levels of dispersion than distal genes, though the effect is small and may be due to chance (p=0.053).
claims.source: We found that the set of genes nearest to these trans-species SNPs have higher median levels of dispersion than distal genes, though the effect is small and may be due to chance (p=0.053, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a marginally significant association.

claims.claim: 37 out of 192 trans-species SNPs have a clear eQTL signal (FDR < 0.1) in the human dataset.
claims.source: We detected 37/192 trans-species SNPs with a clear eQTL signal (FDR < 0.1) in the well-powered human dataset, such as rs257899, which associates with SLC27A6 expression.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the number of trans-species SNPs with eQTL activity in humans.

claims.claim: No significant cis eQTL activity was identified for rs257899 in chimpanzee.
claims.source: However, we did not identify any significant cis eQTL activity for this SNP in chimpanzee (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of eQTL activity for a specific SNP in chimpanzees.

claims.claim: No inter-species correlation of regulatory effect size estimates was found among the 12 trans-species haplotypes with an eQTL in human that were also tested in chimpanzee.
claims.source: More generally, we did not find any inter-species correlation of regulatory effect size estimates among the 12 trans-species haplotypes with an eQTL in human (FDR < 0.1; Figure 8B) that were also tested in chimpanzee (Methods).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of correlation in eQTL effect sizes across species.

claims.claim: No evidence was found for regulatory effects of trans-species SNPs in chimpanzee compared to control SNPs.
claims.source: Considering all trans-species SNPs, we did not find any evidence for their regulatory effects in chimpanzee, compared to a set of control SNPs (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison of trans-species SNPs to control SNPs in chimpanzees.

claims.claim: Trans-species SNPs have measurable regulatory activity in the human dataset, but it is not significantly different than that of control SNPs.
claims.source: While we found these SNPs to have measurable regulatory activity in the human dataset, it was not significantly different than that of control SNPs (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison of trans-species SNPs to control SNPs in humans.

claims.claim: No compelling evidence was found that trans-species polymorphisms have strong regulatory activity in either species.
claims.source: In summary, we found no compelling evidence that these trans-species polymorphisms have strong regulatory activity in either species.
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings on trans-species polymorphisms.

claims.claim: Inter-individual expression variability is highly correlated in humans and chimpanzees.
claims.source: We found that inter-individual expression variability is highly correlated in humans and chimpanzees.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states a main finding of the study.

claims.claim: Cell type heterogeneity is a major driver of the degree to which gene expression varies in the population.
claims.source: We found that, across genes, cell type heterogeneity is a major driver of the degree to which gene expression varies in the population.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states a key finding about sources of variability.

claims.claim: Natural selection has played a role in shaping inter-species similarities and differences in gene expression variability.
claims.source: Notwithstanding these complications, our observations do indicate that natural selection has played a role in shaping inter-species similarities and differences in gene expression variability.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion about the role of selection.

claims.claim: Differences in cellular composition cannot explain the observed correlation between dispersion and measures of nucleotide divergence and diversity.
claims.source: Differences in cellular composition cannot explain the observed correlation between dispersion and measures of nucleotide divergence and diversity.
claims.evidence: The manuscript argues that cellular composition cannot fully explain certain observations.

claims.claim: The observation that species-specific eGenes have higher variability in the species in which the eQTL was detected directly points to a genetic basis for differences in expression dispersion between humans and chimpanzees.
claims.source: With that in mind, our observation that species-specific eGenes have higher variability in the species in which the eQTL was detected is significant, because it directly points to a genetic basis for differences in expression dispersion between humans and chimpanzees.
claims.evidence: The manuscript interprets the significance of the eGene-dispersion association.

claims.claim: Genetic variation within species contributes to the overall inter-species divergence in gene regulation.
claims.source: This observation is also consistent with the notion that genetic variation within species contributes to the overall inter-species divergence in gene regulation.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Stronger signals of coding selection were observed for non-eGenes than eGenes in both species.
claims.source: That said, we also observed stronger signals of coding selection for non-eGenes than eGenes in both species, further suggesting selection on the eGenes themselves (this is not expected if our observations are to be explained by differences in cellular composition).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an observation and provides an interpretation.

claims.claim: eQTLs may be a subtle indicator of dosage insensitivity for relatively neutrally evolving genes.
claims.source: Collectively, our observations suggest that, across species, eQTLs may be a subtle indicator of dosage insensitivity for relatively neutrally evolving genes.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from multiple observations.

claims.claim: An inter-species analysis of population variability in gene expression may be a relatively simple way to complement existing methods to assess differences in selection pressures between lineages.
claims.source: Thus, we believe that an inter-species analysis of population variability in gene expression may be a relatively simple way to complement existing methods to assess differences in selection pressures between lineages.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes a methodological contribution based on the findings.

claims.claim: The eGenes identified only in chimpanzee are slightly enriched for transcription regulatory processes.
claims.source: Interestingly, the eGenes we identified only in chimpanzee, but not in human, are slightly enriched for transcription regulatory processes, reminiscent of a previous observation that transcription factors seem to be enriched among the genes positively selected for in the human lineage (Blekhman et al., 2008; Gilad et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports an enrichment result and relates it to prior literature.

claims.claim: Genes involved in immune response are among the most variably expressed and strongly enriched among species-shared eGenes in both human and chimpanzee.
claims.source: In both human and chimpanzee, we found that genes involved in immune response are among the most variably expressed and strongly enriched among species-shared eGenes.
claims.evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about immune genes.

claims.claim: The enrichment of immune genes is consistent with diversifying selective pressure on immune related cell-surface receptor genes to combat diverse and evolving pathogens.
claims.source: This is consistent with a body of literature (Croze et al., 2016; Ejsmond and Radwan, 2015; Hagai et al., 2018; Shultz and Sackton, 2019) that points to diversifying selective pressure on immune related cell-surface receptor genes to identify and combat diverse and ever-evolving pathogens.
claims.evidence: The manuscript interprets the immune gene enrichment in the context of prior literature.

claims.claim: The extent to which quantitative regulation of gene expression is functionally important to pathogen defense and thus the target of selection is unclear.
claims.source: However, the extent to which quantitative regulation of gene expression is functionally important to pathogen defense and thus the target of selection is unclear.
claims.evidence: The manuscript acknowledges uncertainty about the functional importance of regulatory variation.

claims.claim: Regulatory variants may be hitchhiking with functionally important and tightly linked coding variants under strong positive or balancing selection.
claims.source: Alternatively, these regulatory variants may be hitchhiking with functionally important and tightly linked coding variants under strong positive or balancing selection (D'Antonio et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2018; Shiina et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes an alternative explanation with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The study may be underpowered to detect subtle conserved regulatory effects in chimpanzee.
claims.source: We acknowledge that we may be underpowered to detect subtle conserved regulatory effects in chimpanzee.
claims.evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claims.claim: Some trans-species polymorphisms may have important regulatory functions that are tissue-, cell-type-, or context-dependent.
claims.source: Moreover, some of these trans-species polymorphisms may have important regulatory functions; albeit this function may also be tissue-, cell-type-, or context-dependent and not present in our assessment of heart and other GTEx bulk tissues.
claims.evidence: The manuscript acknowledges the possibility of context-dependent regulatory effects.

claims.claim: A deeper understanding of differences in selection on gene expression may be gained by assessing mean differences, variability, and eQTL contributions in various tissue types across primate groups.
claims.source: In summary, we performed a comparative assessment of expression variability and eQTL mapping and found signatures of stabilizing selection on gene regulation in both species. A deeper understanding of differences in selection on gene expression may be gained by further assessing mean differences, variability, and eQTL contributions in various tissue types across primate groups.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes future research directions.

claims.claim: Future studies may benefit from single-cell techniques due to strong contributions of cell-type heterogeneity in the analysis of variability.
claims.source: Such studies may benefit from single-cell techniques, as we find strong contributions of cell-type heterogeneity in our analysis of variability, which may be biological or technical in nature.
claims.evidence: The manuscript recommends methodological approaches for future studies based on the findings.

results.result: The study analyzed RNA-seq data from 39 human and 39 chimpanzee heart tissue samples, combining previously published data with newly generated samples from both species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 clearly document the sample composition and data sources. The manuscript explicitly states sample sizes, tissue types, and data provenance with appropriate citations (C2) and describes new data generation (C4). This is well-documented methodological information.

results.result: The study design introduces technical batch effects partly confounded with species, but these are expected to have minimal impact because the analysis focuses on within-species comparisons, and samples primarily separate by species rather than batch in PCA and clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 acknowledge batch effects (C5) but provide reasoning (C6) and empirical evidence from PCA/clustering (C7) that species differences dominate over technical factors. The logic is sound: within-species analyses for dispersion and eQTLs would be less affected by between-species batch confounding.

results.result: The study identified 8,880 differentially expressed genes between species and performed power analyses demonstrating that sample size (not sequencing depth) drives detection power, that small studies are underpowered but have well-calibrated false discovery rates, and that effect sizes in small studies are upwardly biased due to winner's curse.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C15 report differential expression results and comprehensive subsampling analyses with appropriate statistical frameworks. The power analysis methodology is sound, using the full dataset as a reference standard. The observations about winner's curse (C14) are supported by citations and empirical data. FDR calibration (C15) is empirically validated.

results.result: Some chimpanzee samples are first-degree relatives, but variance partitioning and subsampling analyses show that technical factors like RNA extraction batch explain more variance than relatedness, and inter-relatedness has minimal impact on differential expression results.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 acknowledge relatedness (C16), quantify its contribution via variance partitioning (C17), and empirically test its impact through subsampling (C18). The analyses appropriately address a potential confound and provide evidence it does not substantially affect conclusions.

results.result: Gene expression variability was quantified using a negative binomial model to estimate overdispersion, which was then mean-corrected to obtain 'dispersion' estimates. This identified 2,658 differentially dispersed genes between species, which are generally not differentially expressed, and dispersion is well-correlated between humans and chimpanzees (R=0.60).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 describe a statistically sound approach to quantifying variability. The negative binomial model (C19) is appropriate for RNA-seq count data with theoretical and empirical support (citations provided). The mean-correction procedure (C21) is clearly described. The finding that differential dispersion is independent of differential expression (C23) is important and supported by supplementary data.

results.result: Lower gene expression dispersion is associated with higher protein coding conservation (measured by amino acid identity, dN/dS, and loss-of-function intolerance), with the strongest effects in immune function genes. Housekeeping genes have low dispersion while cardiovascular genes and TATA box genes have high dispersion.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 report associations between dispersion and multiple independent measures of evolutionary constraint with appropriate statistical tests. The use of multiple conservation metrics (C25, C27) and functional enrichment analyses (C26, C30, C31) provides converging evidence. The observation about TATA box genes (C28) is consistent with prior literature (citations provided), though an alternative explanation is acknowledged (C29).

results.result: Dispersion is strongly correlated with cell-type-specificity (R=0.32, p<2×10⁻¹⁶) based on comparison with mouse single-cell RNA-seq data, with highly dispersed genes showing cell-type-specific expression and low dispersion genes showing even expression across cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 report a statistically significant correlation between bulk dispersion and single-cell-derived cell-type-specificity. The analysis appropriately uses the τ statistic (C34) with proper citations. The manuscript acknowledges a limitation (C35) that using mouse data may underestimate the true correlation, showing appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Cell type deconvolution shows qualitatively similar proportions between species with inter-individual variation. Deconvoluted expression profiles cluster by cell type while dispersion estimates cluster more strongly by species, suggesting both genetic differences and cell type heterogeneity drive inter-individual dispersion.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 report results from cell type deconvolution analysis using BayesPrism. The observation that expression clusters by cell type (C37) while dispersion clusters by species (C38) is internally consistent and supports the interpretation (C39) that genetic factors contribute to dispersion beyond cell composition effects.

results.result: Analysis of matched tissue samples from different heart regions shows that individual-level factors explain more variance in cell type composition than tissue-level factors, providing evidence that dispersion estimates reflect true biological differences between individuals rather than technical variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 use an independent dataset (GTEx matched tissues) to validate that cell composition differences are biologically meaningful. The variance partitioning approach (C41) with linear mixed models is appropriate and properly cited. The interpretation (C42) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Inter-species differences in dispersion show weak correlation with cell-type-specificity (R=0.07) and are enriched for mitotic regulators in humans (possibly reflecting GTEx sample characteristics) and immune function genes in chimpanzees.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 report that inter-species dispersion differences are less explained by cell heterogeneity (C43) and show functional enrichments (C44, C46). The interpretation about GTEx samples (C45) is speculative but appropriately caveated with supporting citations about ischemia-induced mitosis.

results.result: High-coverage whole genome sequencing of 39 chimpanzees identified 2.9 million novel SNPs. Analysis of Pn/Ps ratios shows that the inter-species ratio correlates with differences in gene expression dispersion, suggesting inter-species differences in selection pressures at polymorphic loci contribute to dispersion differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 describe new genomic data generation (C48-C49) and analysis linking genetic diversity to expression variability. The Pn/Ps metric (C50-C51) is appropriate for assessing within-species selection. The correlation between Pn/Ps ratio and dispersion difference (C51-C52) provides evidence for a genetic basis of dispersion differences, though the correlation strength is not reported.

results.result: 310 eGenes were identified in chimpanzees with enrichment near transcription start sites. When accounting for power differences through subsampling, there is significant overlap of eGenes between species, with 21 of the top 500 human eGenes also identified in chimpanzees (OR=2.05, p=0.003).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 report eQTL mapping results with appropriate acknowledgment of power differences between species. The subsampling approach (C57) to account for sample size differences is methodologically sound. The significant enrichment (C58) despite modest sample size in chimpanzees is notable and properly tested with hypergeometric test.

results.result: Species-specific eGenes have higher species-specific dispersion (p=3.7×10⁻¹¹), and within each species, eGenes have higher dispersion than non-eGenes. This suggests that genes with eQTLs evolve under less evolutionary constraint.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 report a key finding linking genetic regulation (eQTLs) to expression variability (dispersion) with strong statistical significance (C60). The within-species comparison (C61) provides additional support. The interpretation about evolutionary constraint (C62) is reasonable given the data, though the manuscript acknowledges cell composition could partially explain this.

results.result: eGenes show higher inter-species expression differences and lower coding conservation than non-eGenes. Shared eGenes are enriched for immune response genes including MHC genes, consistent with these genes evolving under strong selection pressures. Chimpanzee-specific eGenes are enriched for transcriptional regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 report multiple lines of evidence that eGenes are under different selective pressures. The associations with differential expression (C63) and coding conservation (C64) are internally consistent. The immune gene enrichment (C65-C66) is well-supported and contextualized with appropriate literature. The transcriptional regulation enrichment (C67) is interesting given prior work on human-specific selection on transcription factors.

results.result: Analysis of 125 trans-species polymorphic haplotypes shows no compelling evidence for conserved regulatory activity in either species, with no correlation of eQTL effect sizes between species and no significant enrichment of regulatory effects compared to control SNPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C75 report negative results from analysis of trans-species polymorphisms. The analysis appropriately uses matched control SNPs (C73-C74) and tests for correlation of effect sizes (C72). The marginally significant association with dispersion (C69, p=0.053) is appropriately described as potentially due to chance. The negative findings are clearly stated (C75) and the manuscript acknowledges power limitations (C90).

results.result: Inter-individual expression variability is highly correlated between humans and chimpanzees, with cell type heterogeneity being a major driver. However, natural selection has shaped variability patterns, as evidenced by correlations with evolutionary constraint measures and the observation that species-specific eGenes have higher species-specific dispersion, pointing to a genetic basis for dispersion differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83 synthesize major findings of the study. The high correlation (C76) and role of cell heterogeneity (C77) are well-supported by earlier results. The conclusion about natural selection (C78) is justified by multiple lines of evidence including conservation metrics (C79) and eQTL-dispersion associations (C80). The interpretation about eQTLs as indicators of dosage insensitivity (C83) is reasonable though speculative.

results.result: The study proposes that inter-species analysis of expression variability can complement existing methods for assessing selection pressures. Immune genes show high variability and enrichment among shared eGenes in both species, consistent with diversifying selection, though whether regulatory variation itself is under selection or hitchhiking with coding variants remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 present interpretations and acknowledge uncertainties. The methodological proposal (C84) is reasonable given the results. The immune gene findings (C86-C87) are well-supported and appropriately contextualized with literature. The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C88) and alternative explanations (C89) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including potential lack of power to detect subtle effects in chimpanzees and possible tissue/context-dependent regulatory functions. Future studies should assess multiple tissues and may benefit from single-cell approaches given the strong contribution of cell-type heterogeneity to variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 appropriately acknowledge study limitations and propose future directions. The power limitation (C90) is relevant given the sample size difference between species. The recommendation for single-cell approaches (C93) is well-justified by the findings about cell heterogeneity throughout the manuscript.
